In the Russian Empire it was ended by decree. At the Synod of Polotsk in February 1839, bishops led by Joseph Semashko declared their church reunited with Russian Orthodoxy. Roughly a million and a half people were moved with a stroke of the pen. The remaining eparchy, Chełm, followed in 1875, and in some villages soldiers broke the resistance by force. What survived did so under Austrian rule in Galicia. There the Greek Catholic Church became more than a church. It was the backbone of Ukrainian national life. Its priests were the teachers, editors and co-op organizers of a people who had almost no other leaders. At the turn of the century Andrey Sheptytsky took the see of Lviv as its metropolitan. His long tenure would carry the church through all that the next fifty years brought.
prose_changes.reason: The fragment 'Its clergy the schoolteachers...' is given a verb. 'Chelm' spelled 'Chełm' as in the summary. 'Broken by force' made active: Pelesz (1880) reports soldiers firing on villagers at Pratulin. Long sentences split for the reading target; no fact added or dropped.

prose_changes.old: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church is the largest Eastern Catholic church in the world today, and everything it survived afterwards — Soviet liquidation in 1946, four decades underground, its re-emergence in 1989. Rested on the Galician base built in this century. In the lands where the union was dissolved by decree, it never came back. The church's habit of carrying a national culture as well as a liturgy, formed here, is still one of the most distinctive things about it.
